text: This lesson closes out the chapter with a wait type that's genuinely different in character: ASYNC_NETWORK_IO. Unlike CPU, I/O, or memory waits, this one usually means the client is the bottleneck, not SQL Server.

ASYNC_NETWORK_IO accumulates when SQL Server has results ready to send, but the send waits because the client hasn't yet consumed the buffer it already holds. It's a measure of the client's consumption rate relative to SQL Server's production rate — not network cable latency.

Row-by-row client processing that does real work between fetches, huge result sets streamed to a thin client instead of aggregated in the query, and SELECT star habits pulling far more data than the client actually uses — all classic causes on the client side.

Check whether the wait is concentrated on a handful of sessions or applications via program_name and host_name, or spread evenly across everything. Concentrated on a few report-tool sessions strongly supports the client explanation; genuinely pervasive across many clients is the rare case worth checking actual network infrastructure for.

The right response almost never involves tuning SQL Server's storage or CPU configuration for this one. Chapter six starts with TempDB — the shared system database every session leans on, and where contention shows up in a very specific, recognizable way.
